newsitem.title: FRANCE: French magistrate urges trial for N-secrets spy.
newsitem.headline: French magistrate urges trial for N-secrets spy.

text.p: A magistrate urged a court on Tuesday to try a French nuclear physicist on charges of selling secrets about France's nuclear arsenal to Moscow at the end of the Cold War, judicial sources said.

Magistrate Roger Le Loire, concluding a four-year probe, told the public prosecutor's office that Francis Temperville, 39, should face charges of spying for the KGB secret service from the late 1980s.
He has been in police custody since 1992 when he was allegedly unmasked by a former Russian diplomat in Paris, Viktor Ochienko, who defected to Britain.

Le Loire's report says Temperville used methods worthy of a spy novel, signalling to his Soviet contacts that he had left secret documents in a Paris rubbish bin by dropping orange peel by a lampost and opening a box of cigarettes.

After reviewing Le Loire's conclusions, a Paris appeal court will decide within two months whether Temperville will face charges of "treason" before a special assize court made up exclusively of professional judges.

Judicial sources said Le Loire's report accuses Temperville of handing about 100 secret documents to two KGB agents in Paris when he was employed as an engineer at the French Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) near Paris.
In exchange, the report says he was paid between 1.0 and 2.0 million francs ($185,000 to $370,000).
The sources said he admitted receiving just 40,000 francs ($7,400). At the time of his detention, the Interior Ministry said Temperville admitted supplying information to a Russian agent.
The secrets included details of French nuclear testing in the South Pacific and a classified yearbook of the military branch of the CEA, the sources said.
Temperville was contacted by the KGB in 1987 after he advertised that he was looking for work as a teacher. The KGB urged him to get a job at the CEA, which he managed in 1989 after about 30 tries.

His original contact at the KGB was Sergei Jmyrev, second secretary at the Soviet embassy in Paris. From 1991, his contact was Valentin Makarov, a third secretary at the Russian delegation at UNESCO in Paris.
Both diplomats have since left France.

Temperville allegedly had an easy time obtaining secrets, merely photocopying documents at work or taking them home in a plastic bag. One judicial source said the case cast doubts on security checks at the CEA.

In 1990, he was forced to resign from the CEA when investigators discovered he was stealing office supplies and sending them, with postage paid by the CEA, to his mother in northern France who owned a stationer's shop.
